fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, actually, partly because of how my own work has been received over the years.

So the honest answer is that, all else equal, a method that works across domains is more valuable. That is almost tautological. If something transfers from vision to language to speech, it is telling you something about learning itself and not just about the structure of one kind of data. The research community rewards that, and I think it should.

But I would push back on the framing a little, because in practice "all else" is almost never equal, and I think people over-apply this criterion in a few ways.

The first is that generality is a claim that is very hard to actually establish. When someone says a method works across domains, often what they mean is they ran it on three benchmarks that happen to be in three different areas. That is not the same as it working across domains. A lot of things that looked universal in 2017 or 2018 ended up being pretty specific to a particular scale or a particular training recipe. And conversely, a lot of things that were dismissed as "just a vision trick" turned out to encode something real. So I am a bit skeptical of judging the value by the breadth claim at the time of publication. The breadth gets revealed later, through other people's work, not by the original authors adding one more table.

The second thing is that domain-specific work is where most of the real understanding comes from. If you look at how a general idea actually gets discovered, it is almost always someone looking very carefully at one problem, noticing something weird, and explaining it. The generalization step comes after. So if we only value cross-domain methods, we are kind of eating the seed corn. You need people who go deep into one domain and are willing to be wrong about whether it transfers.

The third point, and this is a more personal one, is that I think people confuse "works in one domain" with "has no insight." Those are different. I would much rather read a paper that works only on, say, images, but gives me a clear mechanistic story for why, than a paper that works on five domains and the explanation is basically "we tried it and the number went up." The first one changes how I think. The second one just adds a tool to the box, which is fine, but it is a different kind of contribution.

So if I had to give you a rule, I would say: judge by the quality of the understanding first, and the breadth second. Breadth is a multiplier on understanding, not a substitute for it. A deep insight in one domain is worth more than a shallow trick that happens to transfer, because the deep insight will eventually transfer too, once someone figures out the right abstraction.

Where I would get worried is the reverse case, where the method only works in one domain and there is no understanding of why. That is usually a sign that it is fitting the idiosyncrasies of the benchmarks, and those contributions tend to have a very short shelf life. That is the thing to avoid, not domain-specificity per se.

opus-5.5.text:
I tend to value methods that work across domains more highly, though not unconditionally.

If you look at the ideas that really lasted in deep learning, like residual connections, normalization layers, Adam, attention, and the Transformer, almost none of them were tied to a single domain. Many were *discovered* in one domain. ResNet came out of vision and the Transformer came out of machine translation. But they turned out to be about something more basic: how you get signals and gradients through a deep network, or how you let tokens communicate. That's why they spread everywhere. So the impact of a general method compounds. Every new field that adopts it multiplies its value.

Domain-specific methods often have a shorter shelf life. A lot of clever tricks that exploit a particular structure in a particular benchmark get washed away once someone scales up a more generic model with more data and compute. That's the "bitter lesson" story, and I think it's largely been borne out over the past ten years.

That said, I don't think domain-specific work is less valuable by default. There are a few cases where I think it's clearly worth it.

First, when the domain itself matters enormously. If your method solves protein structure prediction, it doesn't matter that it doesn't help image classification. The impact on that field is big enough on its own.

Second, when the domain-specific method reveals something general. Sometimes you solve a problem in one setting, and the insight underneath it transfers even if the exact implementation doesn't.

Third, when it's a stepping stone. Specialized solutions often show what's possible and set a target that more general methods later reach.

In practice, when I evaluate a method, including my own, I ask a few questions:
- **Why does it work?** Is the reason tied to a quirk of the data or benchmark, or to something more fundamental about learning or optimization?
- **Does it survive scale?** If the gain disappears when you train bigger models on more data, I'm skeptical.
- **Is it simple?** Simple methods tend to generalize. If something needs many domain-specific knobs to work, that's often a sign it's fitting the setting rather than capturing a principle.

When we've worked on architectural components, we've tried to test them beyond the domain where we first developed them: vision, language, sometimes speech or other modalities. If it holds up across those, I'm much more confident we found something real. If it only works in one place, it might still be useful, but I'd describe it more modestly.

So my short answer: generality is a strong signal of fundamental value, but domain-specific work can be just as important when the domain is important enough or when it points toward something more general.

fable-5.text:
I think both can be valuable, but I'd say I personally have a strong preference for methods that generalize across domains, and I think the field as a whole tends to reward them more in the long run too.

If you look at the history of deep learning, the ideas that really lasted are the ones that are almost embarrassingly general — things like residual connections, normalization layers, attention, dropout. They're not tied to vision or language or speech specifically. They're more like principles about how to train or structure networks, and that's exactly why they survived all the architecture shifts we've been through. So when I evaluate a method, one question I always ask is: is this exploiting something fundamental about learning, or is it exploiting something about this particular benchmark or data distribution?

That said, I don't want to dismiss domain-specific methods, because they serve two important purposes. First, in the near term, they're often what actually solves the problem. If you're working on medical imaging or protein structures, a method that deeply exploits the structure of that domain can be far more effective than a generic one, and real applications matter. Second — and this is maybe underappreciated — domain-specific methods are often where general ideas come from. Convolutions started as a vision-specific inductive bias, and the lessons we learned from them informed how we think about architecture design everywhere. So a domain-specific method can be a stepping stone; the generality sometimes only becomes clear later.

Where I get more skeptical is when a method is specific not to a domain, but to an experimental setup — it only works at a certain scale, with certain hyperparameters, on a certain benchmark. That kind of specificity usually doesn't age well. Some of my own work has been about going back and re-examining methods like that, and often you find the gains come from confounding factors rather than the core idea.

So maybe my honest answer is: I judge a method less by how many domains it works in today, and more by whether the underlying insight is simple and fundamental enough that I'd expect it to transfer. A simple idea that works in one domain for a clear reason is often more valuable than a complicated one that's been tuned to work in three.

opus-5.text:
Generality isn't really what I value — it's a proxy for something else, which is whether you've found something true. A method that works in five domains is usually telling you that the underlying mechanism is real, not an artifact of one dataset's quirks. That's why we reach for it as a signal.

But it's a noisy proxy in both directions. A lot of papers that claim to work "across domains" are quietly re-tuning hyperparameters for each one, and at that point you haven't shown generality, you've shown that your method has enough knobs to fit anything. I'd rather see one domain studied carefully, with the baseline actually tuned as hard as the proposed method, than six domains done sloppily. We ran into this with pruning — once you train the baseline properly, a lot of the reported gains just evaporate. That kind of finding is narrow, but it changes how you read an entire literature.

And the reverse case matters too. Something tested in one domain might be perfectly general and just untested, because the author only had vision benchmarks on hand. That's a difference in the paper, not in the idea.

So what I actually look at is the reason the method works. If the explanation only makes sense given something peculiar about that domain — the structure of protein sequences, say — then fine, it's a domain contribution, and it should be evaluated as one, which means asking whether that domain is important enough to be worth the specialization. If the explanation is about optimization, or scaling behavior, or architectural inductive bias, then it should transfer, and I get suspicious when it doesn't. That failure is often where the interesting thing is hiding.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think both are valuable, but I judge them by different questions.

For a method that works only in a specific domain, I ask how much that domain matters and how big the gain is. If it solves a real problem in medicine, robotics, or some scientific field, I don't need it to generalize. Being useful in one place is enough. The risk is that a lot of domain-specific work is really fitting to a particular benchmark or dataset, and then it's hard to tell whether it's a real advance or just a good fit to that setting.

For a method that works across domains, I ask whether it's actually general or whether it has only been tested in two or three similar settings. Generality is easy to claim and hard to show. The strongest cases are usually simple ideas that keep working when you change the architecture, the data, or the modality. If something works across many settings without much tuning, that tells me it captures something fundamental and not an accident of one setup.

I'm also wary of treating the two as opposites. A lot of general methods started as domain-specific tricks that people later noticed worked elsewhere. And a general method is often only the right starting point. To get the best result in a particular domain, you usually still need to adapt it.

So my rough rule is that I'm more impressed when a method is simple and works broadly, because that's rarer and usually teaches us more. But I don't discount a domain-specific method if the domain is important and the improvement is real. What I try to avoid is judging a method only by the headline number, without asking why it works and where it would break.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think it depends on what the method is trying to explain. A domain-specific method earns its place if it reveals something about how that domain is structured that a general approach would miss, or if it solves a problem people in that field care about by a margin that matters. A narrow method that teaches you why a domain behaves the way it does can be worth more than a general one that moves a benchmark by a point.

Cross-domain methods have a real appeal, and I don't want to undersell it. If something transfers across vision, language, and audio, that's evidence it's capturing something more fundamental. But generality can also be cheap. If a method only looks universal because every test uses similar setups, breadth is just breadth. So I ask how large the gain is over a strong baseline, and whether it holds when I change the setting in a way that should break it.

A test I find useful is whether the insight can be stated without mentioning the domain. If it can, the narrow result is probably an early version of a broader idea. If it can't, it may still be an excellent contribution, just a different kind, and it should be judged by different standards.

The history of this field has plenty of methods that looked narrow at first and became foundational, and plenty of general-sounding ones that faded. So I try not to put too much weight on either scope or headline claims.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think working across domains automatically makes a method more valuable. If a method works in one domain, but that domain is important and the improvement is substantial, that can be a very valuable contribution. Sometimes exploiting the structure of a particular problem is exactly what makes a good solution possible.

But a method that works across domains gives you a different kind of value. It suggests you’ve captured something more general, and other researchers may be able to build on it in ways you didn’t anticipate.

So I would look at both the impact and what we learn. How much does it help? Why does it work? Do we understand its limitations? A narrow method can give us a broad insight, too. I’d be more interested in those questions than simply counting how many domains someone has tested.

sol-6.1.text:
I think generality is one dimension of a method’s value, but it’s not the only one. If you solve an important problem in one domain, that can already be a very meaningful contribution. Sometimes the method works precisely because it uses structure that’s specific to that domain, and that’s a strength.

At the same time, if a simple idea works across very different domains, that’s exciting because it suggests we’ve captured something more fundamental. It also makes the idea useful to more people.

So I would look at both the importance of the problem and what we learn from the solution. For a specialized method, can we understand why it works there and where its assumptions break? For a general method, does it actually provide a substantial benefit in each setting? I wouldn’t judge the contribution just by counting how many domains it works in.
